extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, rhetoric, and critical reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and diagnostics for identifying logical fallacies in argumentation (generalization, ratiocination, and confusion/ambiguity), with complementary guidance and illustrative examples. Useful for evaluating the soundness of premises, the form of inferences, and the stability of term-meanings across an argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor is not an argument
rubrics_metrics.description: A metaphor is not to be considered as an argument, but as an assertion that an argument exists; that a parity subsists between the case from which the metaphor is drawn and that to which it is applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept figurative illustration as proof. Check for a genuine parity (often a resemblance of relations) between the source and target cases. Example anti-pattern: Bacon’s river/’froth and straws’ illustration — no parity of cause; changing 'levity' to 'buoyancy' exposes the absence of real analogy. Metaphor may indicate a putative argument but does not substitute for showing the actual grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad classification produces fallacies of generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Bringing together under one name things which have no common properties, or only unimportant resemblances, leads to worthless general propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the class named truly shares relevant properties. Beware extension of common-use words by slight links of connection to cases where the defining fact does not exist. Example: Bacon’s critique of the notion 'Humidum' shows how aggregating heterogeneous phenomena under one term yields misleading generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of abstract terms (Idola temere et inæqualiter ā rebus abstractæ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract terms formed 'temere et inæqualiter' (rashly and unequally) from familiar phenomena may aggregate diverse properties into a confused notion that bears no stable relation to reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a term denotes a confused collection of different actions or properties (e.g., 'Humidum' in medieval physics), arguments using that term are suspect. Require precise definition and verification before generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use syllogistic form to reveal ratiocinative fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules of the syllogism are a complete protection against many fallacies of ratiocination; showing reasoning in syllogistic form helps discover bad inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If premises are formally set out (syllogism), fallacies become easier to detect. The exercise forces the reasoner to commit to the premises they must defend. However, lack of formalisation often conceals fallacies — insist on explicit premises when evaluating arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple conversion error (universal affirmative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Erroneous simple conversion of a universal affirmative: treating 'All A are B' as if 'All B are A'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect this common implicit error by checking whether the converse follows logically (it generally does not). Often committed silently in thought rather than explicit speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous conversion of hypothetical (affirming the consequent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistaking the converse of a hypothetical: treating 'If consequent then antecedent' as valid. The proper converse is: 'If the consequent be false, the antecedent is false.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for the fallacy 'If consequent true, antecedent true' (affirming the consequent). Avoid using a true conclusion as proof of the truth of premises; true consequences do not guarantee the truth of a hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusing contrary with contradictory
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to distinguish contrary propositions (which can both be false) from contradictory ones (which cannot both be true/false in the same way).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remind reasoners of the logical canon: contraries may both be false. Forcing the error to be expressed explicitly (putting the contrary/contradictory into words) is effective for detection and exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicious syllogism (more than three terms/undistributed middle/illicit process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogistic fallacies typically arise from having more than three terms, an undistributed middle term, or an illicit process of one of the extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a syllogism, check term distribution and count terms. If premises are not explicitly set out, be alert to hidden extra terms or undistributed middles. The rules of syllogism indicate exactly what must be defended to sustain the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changing premises between linked inferences (à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors that slip in when a chain of reasoning uses a proposition proved under qualification (secundum quid) as if it were true absolutely (simpliciter), losing essential limitations or conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace that the same proposition (including its qualifications and conditions) is used consistently across steps. Examples: Mercantile theory misapplies the maxim 'whatever brings in money enriches' without its provisos; arguments about tithes and rent conflate conditional premises with unconditional conclusions. Common anti-pattern: omission of temporal or contextual conditions when reusing premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misapplication of abstract truths (in the abstract vs absolutely)
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking a principle that is true 'in the abstract' (when modifying causes are absent) and reasoning from it as if it were universally and unconditionally true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether modifying causes or contextual conditions are present; if so, the 'abstract' principle may not apply. This misapplication is especially prevalent and harmful in politics and social reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy of ambiguity (ambiguous terms / shifting senses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Error arising when something true under one sense of a word is reasoned to be true under a different sense—occurs as ambiguous middle or when a term is used in different senses in premises and conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify middle terms and verify they have the same meaning in all occurrences. Check that every term preserves its sense from premises to conclusion; ambiguity of terms frequently undermines apparent logical validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous middle / Fallacia Figuræ Dictionis (paronymous word-shifts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fallacy built on grammatical structure where paronymous or conjugate words (substantive, adjective, verb from same root) are assumed to have precisely corresponding meanings, producing an apparent but invalid inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for shifting grammatical forms (e.g., 'to commit murder' vs 'murderer') and for assuming equivalence between derived forms (project/projector, presume/presumption). The smaller the sense-variation, the more dangerous and harder to spot the fallacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Etymology fallacy (using etymological sense instead of customary sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that the 'right' or original meaning of a word (etymological) should determine its current logical import, thereby distorting ordinary/legal/customary usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer established law, custom, or current usage when interpreting terms in argument; example: 'representative' is treated by sophists as an exact 'spokesman' by etymology, contrary to law/custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polysemy in key technical terms (commerce example: 'money')
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to disambiguate different senses of a technical term leads to erroneous inference — e.g., 'money' meaning either 'currency' (circulating medium) or 'capital seeking investment' (loanable funds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a term has domain-specific senses, require the arguer to specify which sense is intended. Policy or remedial measures based on the wrong sense will be misguided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of politically loaded phrases ('influence of property')
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a phrase that conflates distinct kinds of influence (respect/gratitude vs coercive fear) can mislead debates about policy (e.g., electoral corruption vs legitimate persuasion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate and label different senses of 'influence' and evaluate the moral/political significance of each before concluding that restraints are unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two senses of 'theory' (proper scientific theory vs mere conjecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confounding 'theory' as the completed result of philosophical induction with 'theory' as mere speculative fancy leads to denigration of legitimate generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'theory' as empirically-grounded generalization (legitimate guide to practice) from 'mere theoretical fancy'; do not reject sound theory on the grounds that speculative 'theorists' err.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of institutional terms ('the Church')
rubrics_metrics.description: A word denoting an institution may be used to mean different sub-groups (e.g., 'the Church' sometimes means clergy, sometimes the whole body of believers), producing false inferences about ownership or rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify institutional reference before inferring legal or moral claims (e.g., property ownership vs usufruct).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronoun/subject ambiguity in metaphysical argument ('I' in Descartes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifts in the reference of pronouns (e.g., 'I' meaning 'my will' vs 'the laws of my nature') produce illicit moves in arguments, undermining claimed inferences about origin or possibility of conceiving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track what 'I' or similar indexicals denote in each premise; ensure consistency of reference or make the shift explicit and justified. Example: Descartes' argument equivocates on 'I made the conception' (will vs natural laws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifting senses in free-will debate (Necessity = Certainty vs Compulsion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'Necessity' sometimes to mean 'Certainty' and sometimes 'Compulsion' causes equivocation and invalid conclusions in debates about freedom and causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require precise definitions of contested metaphysical terms; map out consequences under each sense before concluding about freedom/necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of 'same' (sameness numero vs sameness specie)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusing 'same' used to mean 'indistinguishably alike' (specie) with 'numerically identical' (numero) leads to metaphysical confusions (e.g., Plato's theory of Ideas, Berkeley's error about ideas persisting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish similarity (degree/admitted degrees) from strict numerical identity; check whether the argument illicitly transfers properties that only hold for numerical identity to cases of resemblance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflating distinct technical measures (force/vis viva/momentum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to recognize that a technical term (e.g., 'force') may be usefully associated with different measurable effects (vis viva vs momentum) leads disputants to argue as if there were a single fact of the matter rather than a terminological choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a dispute revolves around a technical term, ask whether parties mean different measurable consequences. Clarify which effect the term should be associated with before declaring a factual disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity between 'infinite' and 'infinitely divisible' (Achilles and the Tortoise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tacitly assuming that infinite divisibility implies literal infinitude (or infinity of duration) creates paradoxes; 'forever' in the conclusion may mean 'any length of time,' while 'ever' in premises can mean 'any number of subdivisions'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disambiguate 'infinite' contexts: distinguish unlimited divisible subdivision from unbounded magnitude. Resolve apparent paradoxes by clarifying temporal/spatial quantifiers and the intended meaning of 'ever/forever'.
